courses.title: Radiation Protection and Radiobiology
courses.description: Principles and regulation of radiation protection, dose limits, protection of patients, staff and the public, pregnancy, monitoring and radiation emergencies.

topics.title: Principles and Regulation
topics.summary: ICRP principles, ALARA, and radiation regulation in Nigeria.

material.heading: ICRP principles
material.body: The International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) sets three fundamental principles: justification (an exposure must do more good than harm), optimisation (doses kept as low as reasonably achievable — ALARA — taking economic and social factors into account) and dose limitation (occupational and public exposures must not exceed dose limits; patients' medical exposures have no dose limits but are governed by justification and optimisation, supported by diagnostic reference levels — DRLs).

material.heading: Regulation in Nigeria
material.body: The Nigerian Nuclear Regulatory Authority (NNRA), established under the Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection Act (1995), licenses facilities using ionising radiation, inspects them and sets regulations (e.g. Nigerian Basic Ionizing Radiation Regulations). Each facility appoints a radiation safety officer, maintains controlled and supervised areas with warning signs (the trefoil symbol), keeps dose records, performs quality control on equipment, and trains staff. Radiographers are registered by the Radiographers Registration Board of Nigeria (RRBN).
keyPoints: Radiation safety officer in each facility

topics.title: Dose Limits and Personal Monitoring
topics.summary: Occupational and public dose limits, dosimeters and classification of workers and areas.

material.heading: Dose limits
material.body: ICRP recommended limits (adopted in most national regulations): occupational effective dose 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (no more than 50 mSv in any single year); equivalent dose to the lens of the eye 20 mSv/year (reduced from 150 mSv in 2011); skin and extremities (hands, feet) 500 mSv/year. Public: effective dose 1 mSv/year; lens 15 mSv/year; skin 50 mSv/year. For a pregnant worker, once pregnancy is declared, the dose to the fetus should not exceed 1 mSv for the rest of the pregnancy. Workers under 18 have lower limits. Natural background radiation averages about 2.4 mSv/year worldwide.

material.heading: Monitoring
material.body: Personal dosimeters record staff doses: thermoluminescent dosimeters (TLDs — lithium fluoride crystals that emit light on heating in proportion to dose), optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dosimeters, film badges (older) and electronic personal dosimeters (real-time readings). The whole-body dosimeter is worn on the trunk (under a lead apron in some protocols, with a second collar dosimeter outside for eye/thyroid estimation); ring dosimeters monitor extremity dose in fluoroscopy and nuclear medicine. Dosimeters are changed and read periodically (e.g. monthly or quarterly), and records are kept. Survey meters (Geiger–Müller counters, ionisation chambers) measure dose rates and contamination.
keyPoints: TLD: lithium fluoride, read by heating

topics.title: Protecting Staff and the Public
topics.summary: Time, distance and shielding; room design; protective equipment; fluoroscopy and mobile radiography.

material.heading: Time, distance, shielding
material.body: The three basic methods of external radiation protection: minimise time near the source; maximise distance (inverse square law — doubling distance reduces dose rate to a quarter; stand at least 2 metres from the patient during mobile radiography); and use shielding (lead, concrete, barium plaster). X-ray rooms have shielded walls and doors, lead-glass viewing windows, a protected control area, and warning lights ('X-ray in use'). Lead aprons (commonly 0.25–0.5 mm lead equivalent), thyroid collars and lead glasses are worn in fluoroscopy and interventional procedures; they should be stored hung or flat to avoid cracks and checked periodically by fluoroscopy.
keyPoints: Stand ≥ 2 m away in mobile radiography
Lead aprons 0.25–0.5 mm Pb; check for cracks

material.heading: Fluoroscopy and practice
material.body: In fluoroscopy, the main source of staff dose is scatter from the patient; staff should stand on the image-receptor side (for a C-arm with the tube under the table, scatter is highest on the tube side and below the table). Use pulsed fluoroscopy, last-image hold, collimation, minimal screening time, and keep the image intensifier close to the patient. Never hold patients during exposures as routine; if unavoidable, use relatives (not pregnant, not staff repeatedly) with protective clothing, and record it. Never point the primary beam at occupied areas.
keyPoints: Scatter from the patient is the main staff hazard
Staff should not routinely hold patients

topics.title: Protecting Patients, Pregnancy and Children
topics.summary: Patient dose reduction, gonad shielding, pregnancy checks, and paediatric imaging.

material.heading: Patient dose reduction
material.body: Patient doses are reduced by justification (right test, avoid repeats — check previous imaging), correct technique to avoid retakes, tight collimation, appropriate exposure factors (higher kVp with lower mAs where image quality allows), adequate filtration, fast image receptors, avoiding unnecessary views, using immobilisation, and — in CT — automatic exposure control, low-dose protocols and limiting scan range. Alternatives without ionising radiation (ultrasound, MRI) should be considered, especially for children and pregnant women.
keyPoints: CT: dose modulation and low-dose protocols

material.heading: Pregnancy and children
material.body: Women of child-bearing age (usually 12–55 years) must be asked about pregnancy before examinations in which the primary beam irradiates the pelvis or abdomen; if pregnancy cannot be excluded, the examination may be postponed or modified, unless clinically urgent. The fetus is most sensitive to malformations during organogenesis (about 3–15 weeks); risks of deterministic effects are negligible below about 100 mGy fetal dose. A pregnancy should never be terminated because of diagnostic-dose exposure alone. Children are about 2–3 times more radiosensitive than adults and have a longer lifespan in which cancers may develop; use child-sized protocols ('Image Gently'), immobilisation aids and parental reassurance.

topics.title: Quality Assurance, Accidents and Emergencies
topics.summary: Equipment QA, reject analysis, radiation incidents, and managing contamination.

material.heading: Quality assurance
material.body: Quality assurance programmes ensure consistent image quality at the lowest reasonable dose. Tests include kVp accuracy, timer accuracy, output linearity and reproducibility, half-value layer (filtration), light-beam/X-ray field alignment, focal spot size, grid alignment, detector uniformity and, in CT, CT number accuracy and noise. Reject (repeat) analysis identifies causes of repeated images (positioning errors, exposure errors, motion, artefacts) so that training or equipment problems can be corrected — repeats double patient dose.
keyPoints: Tests: kVp, timer, output, HVL, field alignment

material.heading: Incidents and emergencies
material.body: Radiation incidents include unintended or excessive exposures (wrong patient, wrong examination, equipment malfunction), lost or stolen sources and spills of radioactive material. They must be reported to the radiation safety officer and, where required, to the NNRA, investigated and corrected. For a radioactive spill in nuclear medicine: alert others, contain the spill with absorbent material, restrict access, wear gloves and protective clothing, decontaminate from the outside inwards, monitor with a survey meter, and dispose of waste as radioactive. Personnel contamination is removed by washing skin with lukewarm water and mild soap without abrading. Potassium iodide blocks thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine in nuclear emergencies.
keyPoints: Spill: contain, restrict, decontaminate outside-in, monitor
